claim: The striatum is the major input nucleus of the basal ganglia.
source: The striatum is the major input nucleus of the basal ganglia (BG) and contains two major populations of medium spiny projection neurons (Gerfen et al., 1990; Mink, 1996).
evidence: Supported by citations to Gerfen et al., 1990 and Mink, 1996

claim: The striatum contains two major populations of medium spiny projection neurons.
source: The striatum is the major input nucleus of the basal ganglia (BG) and contains two major populations of medium spiny projection neurons (Gerfen et al., 1990; Mink, 1996).
evidence: Supported by citations to Gerfen et al., 1990 and Mink, 1996

claim: Striatonigral (direct pathway) neurons express D1 receptors.
source: Striatonigral (direct pathway) neurons express D1 receptors and project to the substantia nigra pars reticulata (SNr) and other BG output nuclei.

claim: Striatonigral neurons project to the substantia nigra pars reticulata (SNr) and other BG output nuclei.
source: Striatonigral (direct pathway) neurons express D1 receptors and project to the substantia nigra pars reticulata (SNr) and other BG output nuclei.

claim: Striatopallidal (indirect pathway) neurons express D2 receptors.
source: Striatopallidal (indirect pathway) neurons express D2 receptors and project to the external globus pallidus, which in turn inhibits the SNr.

claim: Striatopallidal neurons project to the external globus pallidus, which in turn inhibits the SNr.
source: Striatopallidal (indirect pathway) neurons express D2 receptors and project to the external globus pallidus, which in turn inhibits the SNr.

claim: An influential model casts the direct and indirect pathways in opposing roles with the direct pathway promoting behavior and the indirect pathway suppressing behavior.
source: Given their opposite effects on BG output, an influential model of the striatum casts the direct and indirect pathways in opposing roles with the direct pathway promoting behavior and the indirect pathway suppressing behavior (Albin et al., 1989; Freeze et al., 2013; Kravitz et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to Albin et al., 1989; Freeze et al., 2013; Kravitz et al., 2010

claim: Studies have described concurrent activation of direct and indirect pathways during behavior, suggesting complementary contributions.
source: More recently, however, this view has been questioned by studies that described concurrent activation of these two populations during behavior, suggesting complementary contributions of these two pathways (Cui et al., 2013; Isomura et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to Cui et al., 2013 and Isomura et al., 2013

claim: The lateral or sensorimotor striatum receives topographically organized innervation from the cortex and thalamus.
source: The lateral or sensorimotor striatum receives topographically organized innervation from the cortex and thalamus (Hintiryan et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Hintiryan et al., 2016

claim: Micro-stimulation of different striatal regions results in movements of different body parts.
source: Micro-stimulation of different striatal regions results in movements of different body parts (Alexander and DeLong, 1985).
evidence: Supported by citation to Alexander and DeLong, 1985

claim: The ventrolateral striatum (VLS) has been implicated in orofacial behaviors, including licking, in rats.
source: In rats, the ventrolateral striatum (VLS) has been implicated in orofacial behaviors, including licking (Mittler et al., 1994; Pisa, 1988a; Pisa, 1988b).
evidence: Supported by citations to Mittler et al., 1994; Pisa, 1988a; Pisa, 1988b

claim: Licking behavior is generated by brain stem pattern generators.
source: Although licking behavior is generated by brain stem pattern generators (Travers et al., 1997), BG output can provide top-down regulation of the pattern generators, either directly or via the nigrotectal projections (Deniau and Chevalier, 1992; Redgrave et al., 1992; Rossi et al., 2016; Shammah-Lagnado et al., 1992; Toda et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Travers et al., 1997

claim: BG output can provide top-down regulation of the pattern generators, either directly or via the nigrotectal projections.
source: Although licking behavior is generated by brain stem pattern generators (Travers et al., 1997), BG output can provide top-down regulation of the pattern generators, either directly or via the nigrotectal projections (Deniau and Chevalier, 1992; Redgrave et al., 1992; Rossi et al., 2016; Shammah-Lagnado et al., 1992; Toda et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to Deniau and Chevalier, 1992; Redgrave et al., 1992; Rossi et al., 2016; Shammah-Lagnado et al., 1992; Toda et al., 2017

claim: Stimulation or enhancing dopaminergic signaling in the VLS can generate orofacial behavior, in some cases dyskinetic movements.
source: Stimulation or enhancing dopaminergic signaling in the VLS can generate orofacial behavior, in some cases dyskinetic movements, while dopamine depletion can abolish such behaviors (Delfs and Kelley, 1990; Jicha and Salamone, 1991; Kelley et al., 1988).
evidence: Supported by citations to Delfs and Kelley, 1990; Jicha and Salamone, 1991; Kelley et al., 1988

claim: Dopamine depletion can abolish orofacial behaviors.
source: Stimulation or enhancing dopaminergic signaling in the VLS can generate orofacial behavior, in some cases dyskinetic movements, while dopamine depletion can abolish such behaviors (Delfs and Kelley, 1990; Jicha and Salamone, 1991; Kelley et al., 1988).
evidence: Supported by citations to Delfs and Kelley, 1990; Jicha and Salamone, 1991; Kelley et al., 1988

claim: Self-initiated behaviors can be precisely timed relative to some anticipated event like a reward.
source: One important characteristic of self-initiated behaviors is that they can be precisely timed relative to some anticipated event like a reward (Gibbon et al., 1984; Pavlov, 1927; Roberts, 1981).
evidence: Supported by citations to Gibbon et al., 1984; Pavlov, 1927; Roberts, 1981

claim: The BG have been implicated in interval timing in the seconds to minutes range.
source: The BG have been implicated in such interval timing in the seconds to minutes range (Buhusi and Meck, 2005; Merchant et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to Buhusi and Meck, 2005; Merchant et al., 2013

claim: Manipulation of dopamine activity can bidirectionally influence estimation of the passage of time.
source: Manipulation of dopamine activity can bidirectionally influence estimation of the passage of time (Buhusi and Meck, 2005; Meck, 1996) and lesions of the striatum also impair timing behavior (Meck, 2006).
evidence: Supported by citations to Buhusi and Meck, 2005; Meck, 1996

claim: Lesions of the striatum impair timing behavior.
source: Manipulation of dopamine activity can bidirectionally influence estimation of the passage of time (Buhusi and Meck, 2005; Meck, 1996) and lesions of the striatum also impair timing behavior (Meck, 2006).

claim: Striatal activity has been shown to represent time intervals.
source: Furthermore, striatal activity has also been shown to represent time intervals (Bakhurin et al., 2017; Gouvêa et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to Bakhurin et al., 2017; Gouvêa et al., 2015

claim: AAV5-DIO-ChR2 virus was bilaterally injected in the VLS region of the striatum in D1-Cre and A2A-Cre mice.
source: We bilaterally injected a Cre-dependent AAV5-DIO-ChR2 virus in the VLS region of the striatum in D1-Cre (Figure 1C) and A2A-Cre (Figure 1D) mice and implanted chronic optic fibers just above this area.

claim: Chronic optic fibers were implanted just above the VLS area.
source: We bilaterally injected a Cre-dependent AAV5-DIO-ChR2 virus in the VLS region of the striatum in D1-Cre (Figure 1C) and A2A-Cre (Figure 1D) mice and implanted chronic optic fibers just above this area.

claim: Mice received a 5 μL drop of 10% sucrose solution every 10 s in the fixed-time task.
source: Mice received a 5 μL drop of 10% sucrose solution every 10 s (Figure 1E).

claim: Voluntary licking behavior in all mice consisted of bouts of rhythmic protrusion and retractions of the tongue at a relatively fixed rate (4–8 Hz).
source: Voluntary licking behavior in all mice consisted of bouts of rhythmic protrusion and retractions of the tongue at a relatively fixed rate (4–8 Hz).

claim: Well-trained mice reliably generated anticipatory licking behavior before reward delivery.
source: Well-trained mice reliably generated anticipatory licking behavior before reward delivery (Figure 1F).
evidence: Observation from experimental data shown in Figure 1F

claim: Direct pathway stimulation initiates licking.
source: Direct pathway stimulation initiates licking, whereas indirect pathway stimulation suppresses licking and results in rebound licking after stimulation.
evidence: Main finding from experimental data presented in the manuscript

claim: Indirect pathway stimulation suppresses licking and results in rebound licking after stimulation.
source: Direct pathway stimulation initiates licking, whereas indirect pathway stimulation suppresses licking and results in rebound licking after stimulation.
evidence: Main finding from experimental data presented in the manuscript

claim: Direct pathway stimulation produced a resetting of the internal timing process.
source: Direct pathway stimulation produced a resetting of the internal timing process, whereas indirect pathway stimulation transiently paused timing, and proportionally delayed the next bout of licking.
evidence: Main finding from experimental data on timing behavior

claim: Indirect pathway stimulation transiently paused timing, and proportionally delayed the next bout of licking.
source: Direct pathway stimulation produced a resetting of the internal timing process, whereas indirect pathway stimulation transiently paused timing, and proportionally delayed the next bout of licking.
evidence: Main finding from experimental data on timing behavior

claim: Activation of direct pathway MSNs induced licking when stimulated 5 s before reward delivery.
source: Though licking was sparse at this time point (Figure 2B, top), activation of direct pathway MSNs induced licking (Figure 2B, bottom and Figure 2C, Video 1).
evidence: Observation from experimental data shown in Figure 2B, 2C, and Video 1

claim: A two-way ANOVA revealed a change of licking rate resulting from VLS direct pathway stimulation (main effect of group, F1,44 = 93.6, p<0.0001).
source: A two-way ANOVA (stimulation frequency x experimental group) revealed a change of licking rate resulting from VLS direct pathway stimulation (main effect of group, F1,44 = 93.6, p<0.0001) and a significant effect of laser frequency (F3,44 = 4.64, p<0.01); there was a also an interaction between frequency and group (F3,44 = 4.84, p<0.01).

claim: There was a significant effect of laser frequency on licking rate (F3,44 = 4.64, p<0.01).
source: A two-way ANOVA (stimulation frequency x experimental group) revealed a change of licking rate resulting from VLS direct pathway stimulation (main effect of group, F1,44 = 93.6, p<0.0001) and a significant effect of laser frequency (F3,44 = 4.64, p<0.01); there was a also an interaction between frequency and group (F3,44 = 4.84, p<0.01).

claim: There was an interaction between frequency and group (F3,44 = 4.84, p<0.01).
source: A two-way ANOVA (stimulation frequency x experimental group) revealed a change of licking rate resulting from VLS direct pathway stimulation (main effect of group, F1,44 = 93.6, p<0.0001) and a significant effect of laser frequency (F3,44 = 4.64, p<0.01); there was a also an interaction between frequency and group (F3,44 = 4.84, p<0.01).

claim: Lick rate was significantly increased by 10 Hz (p<0.01), 25 Hz, (p<0.001), and 50 Hz (p<0.001) stimulation of the direct pathway.
source: Post-hoc tests revealed that lick rate was significantly increased by 10 Hz (p<0.01), 25 Hz, (p<0.001), and 50 Hz (p<0.001) stimulation of the direct pathway.

claim: Direct pathway stimulation at 1 s before reward delivery resulted in potentiation of the licking rate.
source: We next stimulated the direct pathway at 1 s before reward delivery (Figure 2E), during the time of maximal anticipatory licking (Figure 2F, top). Although there was a ceiling effect on licking at this time point (Figure 2F, bottom), we regularly observed a potentiation of the licking rate during stimulation when compared to trials without stimulation (Figure 2G).
evidence: Observation from experimental data shown in Figures 2E-G

claim: A two-way ANOVA revealed significant increase in licking as a result of VLS stimulation at 1 s before reward (main effect of group, F1,37 = 48.82, p<0.0001).
source: A two-way ANOVA revealed significant increase in licking as a result of VLS stimulation (Figure 2H, main effect of group, F1,37 = 48.82, p<0.0001), but no effect of frequency (F3,37 = 1.31, p=0.3) nor a significant interaction between frequency and group (F3,37 = 1.79, p=0.16).

claim: Stimulation at the time of reward delivery had a significant effect on licking (F1,36 = 8.65, p<0.01).
source: However, a two-way ANOVA detected a significant effect of stimulation on licking even during consumption (Figure 2L, F1,36 = 8.65, p<0.01), but did not show a significant effect of stimulation frequency (F3,36 = 1.27, p=0.3), nor a significant interaction (F3,36 = 1.73, p=0.18).

claim: A two-way ANOVA revealed significant effects of both the time of stimulation in the task (main effect of time, F3,67 = 9.16, p<0.0001) and laser frequency (F2,67 = 24.31, p<0.0001).
source: A two-way ANOVA revealed significant effects of both the time of stimulation in the task (Figure 2M, main effect of time, F3,67 = 9.16, p<0.0001) and laser frequency (F2,67 = 24.31, p<0.0001), with no significant interaction (F6,67 = 0.99, p=0.44).

claim: Direct pathway stimulation in the orofacial striatum can result in the generation of licking behavior.
source: Together, these results show for the first time that direct pathway stimulation in the orofacial striatum can result in the generation of licking behavior.

claim: The effects of direct pathway stimulation were dependent on the on-going behavioral state of the animals.
source: The effects of direct pathway stimulation were dependent on the on-going behavioral state of the animals, which can be explained by a ceiling effect.

claim: Licking during laser presentation could be shifted rightward toward a frequency of 10 Hz.
source: Remarkably, we observed that it was possible for licking to exceed the frequencies normally produced by mice during direct pathway stimulation (Figure 3A). Licking during laser presentation could be shifted rightward toward a frequency of 10 Hz (Video 2).
evidence: Observation from experimental data shown in Figure 3A and Video 2

claim: 10 Hz appeared to be the upper limit of the central pattern generator for licking.
source: This appeared to be the upper limit of the central pattern generator for licking, as naturally generated licking showed predominant frequencies between 4 and 6 Hz.

claim: Licking frequencies are higher during direct pathway stimulation compared to licking produced during anticipation.
source: We quantified power spectral density (PSD) distributions for licking and observed that licking frequencies are higher during direct pathway stimulation compared to licking produced during anticipation (Figure 3B).
evidence: Analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 3B

claim: There was a significant interaction between stimulation frequency and licking frequency bands (F8,58 = 2.54, p < 0.05) when stimulation occurred 1 second prior to reward.
source: A two-way mixed ANOVA showed that was a significant interaction between stimulation frequency and licking frequency bands (Figure 3D, F8,58 = 2.54, p < 0.05), and significant main effects of both licking frequency band (F2,58 = 15.46, p < 0.0001) and stimulation frequency (F4,58 = 3.89, p < 0.05).

claim: Power in the 8-10Hz band was significantly greater than power in the 4-6 Hz band during 10 (p < 0.05) and 25 (p < 0.01) Hz stimulation.
source: Post-hoc analyses indicated that power in the 8-10Hz band was significantly greater than power in the 4-6 Hz band during 10 (p < 0.05) and 25 (p < 0.01) Hz stimulation and that power in the 6-8 Hz band was significantly greater than in the 4-6 Hz band during 50 Hz (p < 0.01) stimulation.

claim: When stimulation occurred 5 seconds prior to reward, there was a significant interaction between licking frequency band and stimulation frequency (F8,60 = 6.43, p < 0.0001).
source: When stimulation occurred 5 seconds prior to reward, there was a significant interaction between licking frequency band and stimulation frequency (Figure 3E, F8,60 = 6.43, p < 0.0001) in their effects on PSD amplitude.

claim: Light delivery to the VLS resulted in rightward shift in the frequency domain, above the naturally occurring states that mice normally generate.
source: Together, light delivery to the VLS resulted in rightward shift in the frequency domain, above the naturally occurring states that mice normally generate.

claim: Direct pathway stimulation could increase the degree to which of licking occupied a given frequency band, reflected in the shape of the PSD function.
source: In addition, direct pathway stimulation could increase the degree to which of licking occupied a given frequency band, reflected in the shape of the PSD function.

claim: The BG play a role in regulating the frequency and duty cycle of the licking oscillator in different modes corresponding to roughly three frequency bands (4-6 Hz, 6-8 Hz, and 8-10 Hz).
source: These results suggest a role for the BG in regulating the frequency and duty cycle of the licking oscillator in different modes corresponding to roughly three frequency bands (4-6 Hz, 6-8 Hz, and 8-10 Hz).

claim: Licking resulting from direct pathway stimulation at 5 s prior to reward only began after a certain delay.
source: When stimulating the direct pathway at 5 s prior to reward, we observed that licking resulting from stimulation only began after a certain delay (Figure 4A), and that this delay was reduced with higher stimulation frequencies (Figure 4B).
evidence: Observation from experimental data shown in Figures 4A and 4B

claim: A one-way ANOVA revealed a significant effect of stimulation frequency on the latency to initiate licking following the onset of laser stimulation (F3,22 = 4.92, p<0.01).
source: A one-way ANOVA revealed a significant effect of stimulation frequency on the latency to initiate licking following the onset of laser stimulation (Figure 4C; F3,22 = 4.92, p<0.01).

claim: Stimulation resulted in some additional licking even after offset of stimulation, but this was not related to the stimulation frequency.
source: Stimulation would result in some additional licking even after offset of stimulation, but this was not related to the stimulation frequency (Figure 4D; two-way mixed ANOVA; main effect of stimulation, F1,23 = 18.1, p<0.001; main effect of frequency, F3,23 = 3.58, p=0.30; interaction, F3,23 = 1.91, p=0.15).

claim: Greater stimulation of the direct pathway reduces licking initiation latency.
source: These results show that greater stimulation of the direct pathway reduces licking initiation latency, and that licking continues for a short time beyond the immediate period of laser stimulation.

claim: Indirect pathway activation in the VLS in well-trained mice resulted in a pronounced suppression of licking.
source: In contrast to D1 activation, indirect pathway activation in the VLS in well-trained mice resulted in a pronounced suppression of licking.

claim: There was a significant effect of experimental group on the change in licking rate when indirect pathway was stimulated 5 s prior to reward (F1,40 = 12.35, p<0.01).
source: We found a significant effect of experimental group on the change in licking rate (Figure 5D), two-way ANOVA, F1,40 = 12.35, p<0.01), but no effect of frequency (F3,40 = 2.04, p=0.12) nor an interaction between group and frequency (F3,40 = 2.2, p=0.1).

claim: When activating the indirect pathway 1 s prior to reward, there was a strong suppression of licking by indirect pathway stimulation (F1,42 = 35.48, p<0.0001).
source: In addition to a strong suppression of licking by indirect pathway stimulation (Figure 5H), two-way ANOVA; significant effect of experimental group F1,42 = 35.48, p<0.0001), we observed a significant effect of stimulation frequency on licking (F3,42 = 8.88, p<0.0001), and a significant interaction between group and frequency (F3,42 = 6.31, p<0.01).

claim: 25 Hz (p<0.001) and 50 Hz (p<0.001) stimulation of the indirect pathway significantly suppressed licking.
source: Post-hoc tests revealed significant suppression of licking by 25 Hz (p<0.001) and 50 Hz (p<0.001) stimulation.

claim: Indirect pathway stimulation could suppress consummatory licking that occurred following reward.
source: We were also able to suppress consummatory licking that occurred following reward (Figures 5I, J and K).
evidence: Observation from experimental data shown in Figures 5I, J, and K

claim: The effect of indirect pathway stimulation was dependent on the time of stimulation.
source: The effect of indirect pathway stimulation was also dependent on the time of stimulation. A two-way ANOVA revealed significant effects of both time of stimulation in the task (Figure 5M, F3,76 = 21.38, p<0.0001) and laser frequency (F2,76 = 3.19, p<0.05), with no significant interaction (F6,76 = 2.1, p=0.06).

claim: Indirect pathway activation suggests less of an effect on licking occurring during consumption than on licking during anticipation.
source: Furthermore, indirect pathway activation suggests less of an effect on licking occurring during consumption than on licking during anticipation.

claim: When indirect pathway was activated at 5 s prior to reward delivery, a striking rebound of licking was observed following the offset of stimulation.
source: When we activated the indirect pathway at 5 s prior to reward delivery, when mice were least likely to lick, we observed a striking rebound of licking following the offset of stimulation (Figures 4B C, 6A B, Video 4).
evidence: Observation from experimental data shown in Figures 4B, C, 6A, B, and Video 4

claim: Lick rates during rebound were higher during the second following laser offset as compared to the same time point in the absence of stimulation (F1,24 = 11.08, p<0.01).
source: Lick rates during this rebound were higher during the second following laser offset as compared to the same time point in the absence of stimulation (Figure 6C, two-way mixed ANOVA, main effect of stimulation, F1,24 = 11.08, p<0.01), but there was no main effect of frequency (F3,24 = 0.17, p=0.9) and no interaction between stimulation frequency and the rebound licking rate (F3,24 = 0.36, p=0.78).

claim: Indirect pathway stimulation resulted in a reduced latency to initial lick onset following stimulation when compared to non-stimulation trials (F1,24 = 16.41, p<0.001).
source: Indirect pathway stimulation also resulted in a reduced latency to initial lick onset following stimulation when compared to non-stimulation trials (Figure 6D, two-way mixed ANOVA, F1,24 = 16.41, p<0.001; main effect of frequency, F3,24 = 2.85, p=0.05).

claim: Higher frequencies of indirect pathway stimulation resulted in lower onset latencies (F3,24 = 5.73, p<0.01).
source: There was a significant interaction between trial type and the stimulation frequency, with higher frequencies resulting in lower onset latencies (F3,24 = 5.73, p<0.01).

claim: Varying stimulation frequencies resulted in differing effects on the regularity of rebound latencies (F3,24 = 6.12, p<0.01).
source: Varying stimulation frequencies resulted in differing effects on the regularity of rebound latencies, indicated by measuring the variance of lick onset (Figure 6E, two-way mixed ANOVA, main effect of frequency, F3,24 = 6.12, p<0.01; main effect of stimulation, F1,24 = 3.3, p=0.08; interaction between stimulation frequency and trial type, F3,24 = 8.63, p<0.001).

claim: The effects of laser stimulation would be altered over the course of the behavioral session, as a function of motivational state.
source: We observed that the effects of laser stimulation would be altered over the course of the behavioral session, as a function of motivational state.

claim: A two-way, mixed ANOVA revealed a significant interaction between frequency and quartile (F9,72 = 2.62, p<0.05) in their effects on lick rate during direct pathway stimulation.
source: A two-way, mixed ANOVA revealed a significant interaction between frequency and quartile (F9,72 = 2.62, p<0.05) in addition to significant effects of frequency (F3,72 = 9.5, p<0.001) and trial quartile (F3,72 = 3.64, p<0.05) on lick rate.

claim: The latency to stimulation-evoked lick onset increased over time.
source: We also found that the latency to stimulation-evoked lick onset increased over time.

claim: A two-way, mixed ANOVA revealed a significant effect of trial quartile on lick onset latency (F3,60 = 3.25, p<0.05).
source: A two-way, mixed ANOVA revealed a significant effect of trial quartile on lick onset latency (Figure 7E, F3,60 = 3.25, p<0.05) and a significant effect of frequency (F3,60 = 5.67, p<0.01), but no interaction between trial quartile and stimulation frequency (F9,60 = 0.38, p=0.9), suggesting a uniform increase in latency across all parameters.

claim: The latency of rebound licking increased as the mouse became sated in the course of a session.
source: The latency of rebound licking increased as the mouse became sated in the course of a session, but this was most evident at higher stimulation frequencies (Figure 7G, two-way mixed ANOVA, interaction between trial quartile and stimulation frequency F9,72 = 2.16, p<0.05; main effect of frequency, F3,72 = 3.88, p<0.05; main effect of trial quartile F3,72 = 4.04, p<0.05).

claim: Engagement of lower-level licking generators by the BG can be modulated by motivational signals.
source: These results suggest that engagement of lower-level licking generators by the BG can be modulated by motivational signals.

claim: All mice generated anticipatory licking bouts during probe trials.
source: All mice generated anticipatory licking bouts during probe trials.

claim: Averaging across many trials results in a distribution of licking rates whose peak reflects the expected time of reward delivery, at approximately 10 s.
source: Averaging across many trials results in a distribution of licking rates whose peak reflects the expected time of reward delivery, in this task at approximately 10 s.

claim: Stimulation of the direct pathway during the probe trial could shift the peak rightward by an entire interval-duration.
source: We found that stimulation of the direct pathway during the probe trial could shift the peak rightward by an entire interval-duration.

claim: The peak shift is a function of the start time of direct pathway stimulation (F3,9 = 21.68, p<0.001).
source: Indeed, we found that the peak shift is a function of the start time of direct pathway stimulation (Figure 9B, one-way, RM ANOVA; F3,9 = 21.68, p<0.001).

claim: Control mice did not display any shifts in peak timing (F2,8 = 0.7, p=0.5).
source: Control mice did not display any shifts in peak timing (data not shown; one-way RM ANOVA; F2,8 = 0.7, p=0.5).

claim: Direct pathway stimulation reduced the peak width (F1,12 = 35.49, p<0.0001).
source: We found that direct pathway stimulation reduced the peak width, but we did not observe a significant effect of stimulation time on the width (Figure 9C, two-way mixed ANOVA; main effect of stimulation, F1,12 = 35.49, p<0.0001; no main effect of stimulation time, F3,12 = 0.23, p=0.8; no interaction between stimulation time and stimulation, F3,12 = 1.43, p=0.3).

claim: Direct pathway stimulation did not significantly impact the skew of the peak distributions.
source: Direct pathway stimulation did not significantly impact the skew of the peak distributions (Figure 9D).
evidence: Analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 9D

claim: Direct pathway activation plays a critical role in resetting the internal timekeeping mechanism.
source: These results reveal a critical role of direct pathway activation in resetting the internal timekeeping mechanism.

claim: This is the first report of a specific neural correlate of timer resetting.
source: This is the first report of a specific neural correlate of timer resetting.

claim: Stimulation prior to reward did not impact the peak, suggesting that normally reward receipt may be involved in resetting the timing mechanism.
source: Interestingly, stimulation prior to reward did not impact the peak, suggesting that normally reward receipt may be involved in resetting the timing mechanism.

claim: Stimulation of the indirect pathway at 5 s after reward resulted in a rebound in licking following the termination of stimulation during peak probe trials.
source: We also tested the effect of indirect pathway stimulation during probe trials. As observed previously, stimulation of the indirect pathway at 5 s after reward resulted in a rebound in licking following the termination of stimulation. This was also the case during peak probe trials.

claim: Rebound licking could result in a brief delay in licking which was followed by a bout of licking resembling a peak response ('recovery' pattern).
source: Mice showed different types of responses following rebound licking. First, rebound licking would result in a brief delay in licking which was followed by a bout of licking resembling a peak response ('recovery' pattern, Figure 10A).
evidence: Observation from experimental data shown in Figure 10A

claim: Rebound licking could also initiate the peak, so that the peak lasts longer than usual ('initiation' pattern).
source: Moreover, rebound licking could also initiate the peak, so that the peak lasts longer than usual ('initiation' pattern, Figure 10B).
evidence: Observation from experimental data shown in Figure 10B

claim: Mice occasionally generated a peak without showing a clear rebound following stimulation ('no-rebound' pattern).
source: Occasionally mice also generated a peak without showing a clear rebound following stimulation ('no-rebound' pattern, Figure 10C).
evidence: Observation from experimental data shown in Figure 10C

claim: The different patterns (recovery, initiation, and no-rebound) were equally common (F2,8 = 0.6, p>0.05).
source: These different patterns (recovery, initiation, and no-rebound) were equally common (Figure 10D, n = 5, one-way RM ANOVA; F2,8 = 0.6, p>0.05).

claim: During recovery-pattern trials, there was a large rightward shift of the peak that averaged approximately 2 s (t4 = 6.5, p<0.01).
source: During recovery-pattern trials, we found a large rightward shift of the peak that averaged approximately 2 s (Figure 10E, two-tailed t-test, t4 = 6.5, p<0.01).

claim: When licking was initiated by the rebound licking bout, the peak was not affected (t4 = 2, p=0.1).
source: In contrast, we found that when licking was initiated by the rebound licking bout, the peak was not affected (two-tailed t-test, t4 = 2, p=0.1).

claim: On trials that lacked rebound licking, there was a rightward peak shift of approximately 750 ms (t4 = 4.35, p<0.05).
source: On trials that lacked rebound licking, we found a rightward peak shift of approximately 750 ms (two-tailed t-test, t4 = 4.35, p<0.05).

claim: Initiation-type trials showed increased peak duration (t4 = 4.18, p<0.05).
source: Although initiation-type trials did not show a change in peak timing, we found that these peaks showed increased duration (Figure 10F, two-tailed t-test, t4 = 4.18, p<0.05).

claim: There was no significant impact on the skew of the peaks in any trial type.
source: We did not find a significant impact on the skew of the peaks in any trial type (Figure 10G).
evidence: Analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 10G

claim: The probability of the recovery pattern decreased as the session progressed, whereas the likelihood of detecting no-rebound patterns increased (F1,12 = 7.38, p<0.01).
source: The probability of the recovery pattern decreased as the session progressed, whereas the likelihood of detecting no-rebound patterns increased (Figure 10H, two-way, mixed ANOVA; interaction of the effects of trial type and session half, F1,12 = 7.38, p<0.01).

claim: Optogenetic activation of direct-pathway neurons in the VLS can initiate licking.
source: We found for the first time that optogenetic activation of direct-pathway neurons in the VLS can initiate licking (Figure 2), whereas activation of the indirect pathway in this region can terminate licking (Figure 4).

claim: Activation of the indirect pathway in the VLS can terminate licking.
source: We found for the first time that optogenetic activation of direct-pathway neurons in the VLS can initiate licking (Figure 2), whereas activation of the indirect pathway in this region can terminate licking (Figure 4).

claim: The observed effects are distinct from those following activation of the dorsolateral striatum, which produces locomotion and turning behavior.
source: The observed effects are distinct from those following activation of the dorsolateral striatum, which produces locomotion and turning behavior (Bartholomew et al., 2016; Kravitz et al., 2010; Tecuapetla et al., 2014).

claim: BG projections to lower brainstem pattern generators are not required for reflexive orofacial and tongue movements.
source: Although BG projections to lower brainstem pattern generators are not required for reflexive orofacial and tongue movements (Grill and Norgren, 1978), intact BG are required for goal-directed food seeking behavior (Bignall and Schramm, 1974).
evidence: Supported by citation to Grill and Norgren, 1978

claim: Intact BG are required for goal-directed food seeking behavior.
source: Although BG projections to lower brainstem pattern generators are not required for reflexive orofacial and tongue movements (Grill and Norgren, 1978), intact BG are required for goal-directed food seeking behavior (Bignall and Schramm, 1974).
evidence: Supported by citation to Bignall and Schramm, 1974

claim: A subset of GABAergic projections from SNr to the superior colliculus is critical for the initiation and termination of self-paced licking behavior.
source: It has been shown that a subset of GABAergic projections from SNr to the superior colliculus is critical for the initiation and termination of self-paced licking behavior (Redgrave et al., 1992; Rossi et al., 2016; Toda et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to Redgrave et al., 1992; Rossi et al., 2016; Toda et al., 2017

claim: A pause in licking can be caused by increased activity in nigrotectal output.
source: A pause in licking can be caused by increased activity in nigrotectal output (Rossi et al., 2016; Toda et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to Rossi et al., 2016; Toda et al., 2017

claim: The GABAergic output from the SNr can directly innervate the reticular formation.
source: The GABAergic output from the SNr can also directly innervate the reticular formation (Deniau and Chevalier, 1992), which contains regions that are known to be involved in the generation of licking behavior (Travers et al., 1997).
evidence: Supported by citation to Deniau and Chevalier, 1992

claim: The reticular formation contains regions that are known to be involved in the generation of licking behavior.
source: The GABAergic output from the SNr can also directly innervate the reticular formation (Deniau and Chevalier, 1992), which contains regions that are known to be involved in the generation of licking behavior (Travers et al., 1997).
evidence: Supported by citation to Travers et al., 1997

claim: Direct pathway activation may reduce SNr output and indirect pathway activation may increase SNr output.
source: Direct pathway activation may reduce SNr output and indirect pathway activation may increase SNr output.
evidence: Inference based on known circuit anatomy

claim: Brainstem or tectal targets that receive GABAergic SNr projections may be disinhibited by direct pathway activation and suppressed by indirect pathway activation.
source: Consequently, brainstem or tectal targets that receive GABAergic SNr projections may be disinhibited by direct pathway activation and suppressed by indirect pathway activation.

claim: Opponent classes of SNr projection neurons command downstream position control systems in the midbrain and brainstem to move the body in different directions.
source: We previously showed that opponent classes of SNr projection neurons command downstream position control systems in the midbrain and brainstem to move the body in different directions (Barter et al., 2015b; Fan et al., 2012; Yin, 2014b).
evidence: Supported by citations to Barter et al., 2015b; Fan et al., 2012; Yin, 2014b

claim: The direct and indirect pathways play a critical role in modulating the lower level controllers for orofacial behaviors.
source: The present results suggest a critical role of the direct and indirect pathways in modulating the lower level controllers for orofacial behaviors.

claim: The output nuclei of the BG may function as an integrator.
source: A variety of evidence suggests that the output nuclei of the BG may function as an integrator (Barter et al., 2015b; Yin, 2014a; Yin, 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to Barter et al., 2015b; Yin, 2014a; Yin, 2017

claim: The rate of change in the integrator output is proportional to the input magnitude.
source: The rate of change in the integrator output is proportional to the input magnitude.

claim: With continuous control of position, a larger striatal signal is converted to faster rate of change in position control command as well as greater movement amplitude.
source: With continuous control of position, a larger striatal signal (spikes per time window) is converted to faster rate of change in position control command (higher movement velocity) as well as greater movement amplitude (Barter et al., 2015a; Bartholomew et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to Barter et al., 2015a; Bartholomew et al., 2016

claim: The basal ganglia output produces a top-down command from an integrator that influences the operation of the brainstem pattern generator.
source: For licking behavior, we assume that the basal ganglia output also produces a top-down command from an integrator that influences the operation of the brainstem pattern generator.

claim: When the behavior in question is generated by pattern generators with relatively fixed innate rhythms, the mechanism is different from continuous position control.
source: However, when the behavior in question is generated by pattern generators with relatively fixed innate rhythms, the mechanism is different.

claim: The BG output does not modulate the lick frequency in a continuous manner.
source: In this case, the BG output does not modulate the lick frequency in a continuous manner (Rossi et al., 2016), as it is not directly responsible for the generation of each lick.
evidence: Interpretation supported by citation to Rossi et al., 2016

claim: With continuous modulation, lick frequency would linearly scale with direct pathway stimulation frequency, but this was not observed.
source: With continuous modulation, we would expect lick frequency to linearly scale with direct pathway stimulation frequency (Figure 11), but this was not observed.
evidence: Observation from experimental data shown in Figure 11

claim: Once activated, the pattern generator appears to operate in several discrete settings, analogous to a fan with settings like off, low, and high.
source: Once activated, the pattern generator appears to operate in several discrete settings, analogous to a fan with settings like off, low, and high.

claim: Normally, the lick pattern generator oscillates at 5–6 Hz for anticipatory licking and 6–8 Hz for consummatory licking.
source: Normally, the lick pattern generator oscillates at 5–6 Hz for anticipatory licking and 6–8 Hz for consummatory licking.

claim: When the direct pathway was stimulated, licking could reach a new regime (~10 Hz) which appears to be the limit of the lick pattern generator and possibly also the biomechanical constraints of the orofacial musculature.
source: When the direct pathway was stimulated, licking could reach a new regime (~10 Hz) which appears to be the limit of the lick pattern generator and possibly also the biomechanical constraints of the orofacial musculature.

claim: When stimulation frequency exceeded 10 Hz, the licking frequency cannot increase further.
source: When stimulation frequency exceeded 10 Hz, the licking frequency cannot increase further.

claim: BG output may regulate the activity of the lower level lick generators.
source: BG output may regulate the activity of the lower level lick generators.

claim: The integrator is filled by direct pathway activation.
source: The integrator is filled by direct pathway activation.

claim: Direct pathway projections are inhibitory, so the integrator is filled by inhibiting GABAergic nigral neurons, which results in a disinhibition of downstream structures.
source: Because direct pathway projections are inhibitory, the integrator is filled by inhibiting GABAergic nigral neurons, which results in a disinhibition of downstream structures.
evidence: Inference based on known circuit anatomy

claim: Greater activation of the direct pathway produces longer suprathreshold activation of the pattern generator.
source: Greater activation of the direct pathway produces longer suprathreshold activation of the pattern generator (Figure 11B).

claim: The increased power of licking in a given frequency band, indicating longer 'on time' or higher duty cycle of the oscillator, suggests the presence of the integrator.
source: The increased power of licking in a given frequency band, indicating longer 'on time' or higher duty cycle of the oscillator, suggests the presence of the integrator (Figures 3 and 11).
evidence: Interpretation of data shown in Figures 3 and 11

claim: Artificially driving the direct pathway efficiently fills the integrator, which results in saturation and maximum licking rates even at relatively low stimulation frequencies.
source: Artificially driving the direct pathway efficiently fills the integrator, which results in saturation and maximum licking rates even at relatively low stimulation frequencies.

claim: Mice rarely enter the maximum licking regime on their own, perhaps due to the concurrent activity of the indirect pathway.
source: However, mice rarely enter this regime on their own, perhaps due to the concurrent activity of the indirect pathway.

claim: The indirect pathway may play an important role by discharging the integrator, preventing the instantaneous licking frequency from reaching its maximum level in natural licking.
source: The indirect pathway, on the other hand, may play an important role by discharging the integrator, preventing the instantaneous licking frequency from reaching its maximum level in natural licking.

claim: Selective activation of the indirect pathway is equivalent to rapidly reversing the BG output signal, bringing or keeping the pattern generators below their activation thresholds and pausing behavior.
source: Selective activation of the indirect pathway is equivalent to rapidly reversing the BG output signal, bringing or keeping the pattern generators below their activation thresholds and pausing behavior.

claim: It is only under conditions of artificially activating the direct and indirect pathways separately that behavior can be described as operating in an all-or-none, go/no-go fashion.
source: It is therefore only under conditions of artificially activating the direct and indirect pathways separately that behavior can be described as operating in an all-or-none, go/no-go fashion.

claim: Prior observations of coincident activity of the two pathways may reflect coordinated regulation of behavior to keep output within a certain range.
source: Prior observations of coincident activity of the two pathways may reflect coordinated regulation of behavior to keep output within a certain range (DeLong, 1990; Tecuapetla et al., 2014).
evidence: Interpretation supported by citations to DeLong, 1990; Tecuapetla et al., 2014

claim: The balanced relationship between the direct and indirect pathways may be responsible for the continuous adjustments to specific kinematic details of ongoing movement.
source: The balanced relationship between these two pathways may be responsible for the continuous adjustments to specific kinematic details of ongoing movement.

claim: The BG provide top-down modulation of central pattern generators in the form of duty cycle regulation.
source: We propose that the BG provide top-down modulation of central pattern generators in the form of duty cycle regulation.
evidence: Theoretical proposal based on experimental findings

claim: Coordinated activity of the direct and indirect pathways are combined to produce a BG output that modulates how long a relatively stereotyped pattern generator is activated.
source: Coordinated activity of the direct and indirect pathways are combined to produce a BG output that modulates how long a relatively stereotyped pattern generator is activated.

claim: This form of top-down regulation is distinct from the more continuous regulation of position controllers.
source: This form of top-down regulation is distinct from the more continuous regulation of position controllers (Barter et al., 2015b; Yin, 2014b).

claim: Higher frequency indirect pathway stimulation resulted in shorter latency to rebound licking as well as more uniform timing in the start of rebound licking.
source: In addition, higher frequency stimulation resulted in shorter latency to rebound licking as well as more uniform timing in the start of rebound licking.

claim: Indirect pathway stimulation may result in more active nigral output, which results in a large suppression of downstream structures.
source: Indirect pathway stimulation may result in more active nigral output, which results in a large suppression of downstream structures.

claim: The release of inhibition following indirect pathway stimulation gives rise to a burst of rebound activity responsible for lick generation.
source: The release of this inhibition then gives rise to a burst of rebound activity responsible for lick generation, resulting in fast reactivation of licking CPGs above the threshold, and a more consistent latency of the rebound licking.

claim: The effects of stimulation on licking could not be explained as simply a reduction in the efficacy of laser stimulation over the course of a single session because stimulation of the direct pathway at higher frequencies could override the effects of reducing motivation.
source: This could not be explained as simply a reduction in the efficacy of laser stimulation over the course of a single session because stimulation of the direct pathway at higher frequencies could override the effects of reducing motivation.

claim: Over time, the activation threshold for licking increases, blunting the influence of descending signals.
source: These results can be explained by the possibility that, over time, the activation threshold for licking increases, blunting the influence of descending signals.

claim: Some have suggested that the brain's ability to time intervals is an emergent property of sequential neural population dynamics.
source: Some have suggested that the brain's ability to time intervals is an emergent property of sequential neural population dynamics (Bakhurin et al., 2017; Crowe et al., 2014; Mauk and Buonomano, 2004; Mello et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to Bakhurin et al., 2017; Crowe et al., 2014; Mauk and Buonomano, 2004; Mello et al., 2015

claim: Sequential neural population dynamics models do not explain why specific neural circuits are critical for timing.
source: However, these models do not explain why specific neural circuits are critical for timing; nor do they incorporate detailed anatomical organization such as the direct and indirect pathways, which are shown to have distinct roles in timing.

claim: The observations support classic pacemaker-accumulator models.
source: Our observations support classic pacemaker-accumulator models (Gibbon et al., 1984), which contain specific mechanisms that can be paused or reset (Buhusi and Meck, 2002).
evidence: Interpretation supported by citations to Gibbon et al., 1984; Buhusi and Meck, 2002

claim: The proposed BG integrator mechanism is quite similar to the pacemaker-accumulator model, which also makes use of an integrator.
source: In fact, the proposed BG integrator mechanism is quite similar to the pacemaker-accumulator model, which also makes use of an integrator.

claim: Stimulation of the direct pathway can reset the interval timing mechanism.
source: We discovered that stimulation of the direct pathway can reset the interval timing mechanism and activation of the indirect pathway could pause its operation (Figures 9, 10).
evidence: Main finding from experimental data shown in Figures 9 and 10

claim: Activation of the indirect pathway could pause the operation of the interval timing mechanism.
source: We discovered that stimulation of the direct pathway can reset the interval timing mechanism and activation of the indirect pathway could pause its operation (Figures 9, 10).
evidence: Main finding from experimental data shown in Figures 9 and 10

claim: When stimulating the direct pathway during peak probe trials, the peak would appear approximately 10 s following the onset of stimulation.
source: When stimulating the direct pathway, we found that the peak would appear approximately 10 s following the onset of stimulation.

claim: The interval was maintained, but the activation of the direct pathway appeared to reinitiate the accumulation of the 10 s interval, just like resetting some 'internal clock'.
source: The interval was maintained, but the activation of the direct pathway appeared to reinitiate the accumulation of the 10 s interval, just like resetting some 'internal clock'.

claim: Indirect pathway stimulation did not result in a resetting effect, suggesting that resetting is specific to direct pathway activation.
source: On the other hand, indirect pathway stimulation did not result in a resetting effect, suggesting that resetting is specific to direct pathway activation and not a consequence of any distracting neural perturbation.

claim: It is unlikely that the rebound effect is mediated by excessive direct pathway activity.
source: This also makes it unlikely that the rebound effect is mediated by excessive direct pathway activity.

claim: The chief effect of indirect pathway activation appears to be a pause in the timer.
source: In general, the chief effect of indirect pathway activation appears to be a pause in the timer, similar to what has been observed previously with nigrotectal stimulation (Toda et al., 2017).
evidence: Interpretation supported by citation to Toda et al., 2017

claim: Driving the indirect pathway paused the 'clock,' and the presence of rebound licking could extend the duration of the pause.
source: Driving the indirect pathway paused the 'clock,' and the presence of rebound licking could extend the duration of the pause.

claim: The distinct types of trials observed could be explained by variable rates of filling the accumulator.
source: The distinct types of trials observed could be explained by variable rates of filling the accumulator: faster accumulation on a given trial would allow the rebound licking to initiate the peak, whereas with slower accumulation the indirect pathway activity could interrupt or pause this process.

claim: As rebound licking latency increases over time, the proportion of peak-probe trials that contained rebound licking also decreased.
source: In partial support of this idea are our observations of the motivational effects on behavioral responses to indirect pathway stimulation. As rebound licking latency increases over time, the proportion of peak-probe trials that contained rebound licking also decreased.

claim: Direct and indirect pathways can work in concert to continuously regulate ongoing licking.
source: In summary, we show that direct pathway stimulation in the VLS can initiate licking, whereas indirect pathway stimulation can suppress ongoing licking, and that these pathways can work in concert to continuously regulate ongoing licking.

claim: The distinct effects of direct and indirect stimulation on timing behavior suggest that each pathway differentially interacts with the internal time-keeping system.
source: In addition, the distinct effects of direct and indirect stimulation on timing behavior suggest that each pathway differentially interacts with the internal time-keeping system: direct pathway stimulation can reset the timer, whereas indirect pathway activation can only pause or interfere with it.

claim: The presence of distinct mechanisms for resetting and pausing an internal clock could be related to opponent roles of direct and indirect pathways in the integration process.
source: The presence of distinct mechanisms for resetting and pausing an internal clock could be related to opponent roles of direct and indirect pathways in the integration process, akin to the accumulator in timing models.

claim: These results suggest a uniform underlying mechanism that can explain the role of the BG circuits in action generation as well as interval timing.
source: Together these results suggest for the first time a uniform underlying mechanism that can explain the role of the BG circuits in action generation as well as interval timing.

claim: Some have argued that the accumulator is distributed in the cortex.
source: Some have argued that the accumulator is distributed in the cortex (Wang et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Wang et al., 2018

claim: The results suggest that the accumulator resides in the BG output circuit.
source: Our results, however, suggest that it resides in the BG output circuit, though the underlying mechanisms for integration remain unclear.

claim: The underlying mechanisms for integration in the BG output circuit remain unclear.
source: Our results, however, suggest that it resides in the BG output circuit, though the underlying mechanisms for integration remain unclear.

claim: Future work will be necessary to elucidate the neural implementation of the integrator and how the BG output influence and modulate targets in the midbrain and thalamus to regulate performance and timing of actions.
source: Future work will be necessary to elucidate the neural implementation of this integrator and how the BG output influence and modulate targets in the midbrain and thalamus to regulate performance and timing of actions.

claim: We cannot rule out that the same striatal units may be involved in multiple different behaviors depending on context.
source: We cannot rule out that the same striatal units may be involved in multiple different behaviors depending on context.

claim: The head-fixed preparation makes it impossible for other behaviors to be expressed, so the trained behavior, namely licking, may become the prioritized action under this condition.
source: As the head-fixed preparation makes it impossible for the other behaviors to be expressed, the trained behavior, namely licking, may become the prioritized action under this condition.

claim: It would be important in future studies to examine the role of the VLS in unrestrained animals, and the relationship between orofacial behavior and other components of natural appetitive behaviors.
source: It would be important in future studies to examine the role of the VLS in unrestrained animals, and the relationship between orofacial behavior and other components of natural appetitive behaviors.

claim: 8 adult D1-Cre (4 male and 4 female) mice were used.
source: 8 adult D1-Cre (4 male and 4 female) and 13 A2A-Cre (5 male and 3 female mice received ChR2; 2 male and 3 female mice received eYFP injections) mice of both sexes were used (Jackson Labs, Bar Harbor, ME).

claim: 13 A2A-Cre mice were used (5 male and 3 female mice received ChR2; 2 male and 3 female mice received eYFP injections).
source: 8 adult D1-Cre (4 male and 4 female) and 13 A2A-Cre (5 male and 3 female mice received ChR2; 2 male and 3 female mice received eYFP injections) mice of both sexes were used (Jackson Labs, Bar Harbor, ME).

claim: D1-Cre mice have Cre-recombinase targeted to the Drd1a locus.
source: D1-Cre mice have Cre-recombinase targeted to the Drd1a locus, and A2A-Cre mice have Cre-recombinase targeted to the Adora2a.

claim: A2A-Cre mice have Cre-recombinase targeted to the Adora2a locus.
source: D1-Cre mice have Cre-recombinase targeted to the Drd1a locus, and A2A-Cre mice have Cre-recombinase targeted to the Adora2a.

claim: This enabled selective expression in neurons in the direct and indirect pathways, respectively.
source: This enabled selective expression in neurons in the direct and indirect pathways, respectively.

claim: All experiments were conducted during the light phase of the 12:12 light cycle.
source: All experiments were conducted during the light phase of the 12:12 light cycle.

claim: Mice were water deprived and received a 10% sucrose solution during behavioral sessions.
source: Mice were housed in groups of two or three. Mice had unrestricted access to food in their home cages, but were water deprived and received a 10% sucrose solution during behavioral sessions.

claim: Body weight was maintained at 85% body weight and was monitored on a daily basis.
source: Body weight was maintained at 85% body weight and was monitored on a daily basis, with additional water given after experimental training as needed.

claim: All experimental procedures were approved by the Duke University Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee.
source: All experimental procedures were approved by the Duke University Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee.

claim: AAV5-EF1α-DIO-hChR2(H134R)-eYFP was injected into 8 D1-Cre and 8 A2A-Cre mice.
source: AAV5-EF1α-DIO-hChR2(H134R)-eYFP was injected into 8 D1-Cre and 8 A2A-Cre mice.

claim: AAV5-EF1α-DIO-eYFP was injected into 5 A2A-Cre mice for control experiments.
source: AAV5-EF1α-DIO-eYFP was injected into 5 A2A-Cre mice for control experiments.

claim: Vectors were obtained from the University of North Carolina Vector Core.
source: Vectors were obtained from the University of North Carolina Vector Core.

claim: Stereotaxically guided injections of 200 nL per hemisphere were made at AP: +0.2 and ML: 2.5 and DV: −4.6 and −4.4 relative to bregma.
source: Stereotaxically guided injections of (200 nL per hemisphere) were made at AP: +0.2 and ML: 2.5 and DV: −4.6 and −4.4 relative to bregma using a Nanoject III microinjector (Drummond Scientific, Broomall, PA).

claim: 100 µm-core optic fibers were implanted at AP: +0.2, ML: 2.5, and DV: −4.2 to target cell bodies of the VLS.
source: 100 µm-core optic fibers (Precision Fiber Products, Chula Vista, CA) were implanted with the same AP and ML coordinates and at DV: −4.2 in order to target cell bodies of the VLS.

claim: Fibers were secured to the skull with screws and dental cement along with a head post for head fixation.
source: Fibers were secured to the skull with screws and dental cement along with a head post for head fixation.

claim: Mice were allowed 7–14 days to recover from surgery.
source: Mice were allowed 7–14 days to recover from surgery and then were water deprived in their home cages.

claim: A 10% sucrose solution was gravity fed to the spout and its delivery was controlled by the opening of a solenoid valve.
source: A 10% sucrose solution was gravity fed to the spout and its delivery was controlled by the opening of a solenoid valve.

claim: The spout was connected to a capacitance touch-sensor that reported the time of each contact with the spout by the tongue.
source: The spout was connected to a capacitance touch-sensor (MPR121, Adafruit, New York, NY) coupled to an Arduino Leonardo (www.arduino.cc) that reported the time of each contact with the spout by the tongue.

claim: Initial training involved habituation to head-fixation and training mice to collect experimenter-delivered water drops from the spout.
source: Initial training began with water-deprived mice and involved habituation to head-fixation and training mice to collect experimenter-delivered water drops from the spout.

claim: Once reliable licking was established, training began on a fixed-interval version of the task.
source: Once reliable licking was established for drop delivery after a few days, training began on a fixed-interval version of the task.

claim: White noise was played inside of the chamber to mask the sound of the solenoid.
source: White noise was played inside of the chamber to mask the sound of the solenoid (Rossi and Yin, 2015).
evidence: Description of experimental methods supported by citation to Rossi and Yin, 2015

claim: Water was presented at fixed intervals for 200 trials a day until mice showed anticipatory licking behavior.
source: Water was presented at fixed intervals for 200 trials a day until mice showed anticipatory licking behavior.

claim: Peak probe trials occurred with a 60% possibility after three consecutive rewards.
source: Peak probe trials occurred with a 60% possibility after three consecutive rewards.

claim: Peak trials lasted 30 s plus a random duration sampled from a gamma distribution.
source: Peak trials lasted 30 s plus a random duration sampled from a gamma distribution (Matlab function gamrnd using shape parameter = 2.5 and scale parameter = 4).

claim: Optical stimulation occurred both in rewarded and probe trials to prevent mice from predicting the probe trials with the sensation of the stimulation.
source: Optical stimulation occurred both in rewarded and probe trials to prevent mice from predicting the probe trials with the sensation of the stimulation.

claim: Stimulation was pulsed (0.8–2 mW; 5–50 Hz, 10 ms square pulse width, 1 s duration).
source: Stimulation was pulsed (0.8–2 mW; 5–50 Hz, 10 ms square pulse width, 1 s duration).

claim: Stimulation onset was either at −1 s from reward, was concurrent with the time of reward (0 s condition) or occurred 5 s prior to the reward.
source: Stimulation onset was either at −1 s from reward, was concurrent with the time of reward (0 s condition) or occurred 5 s prior to the reward.

claim: During peak probe trials, stimulation was delivered at −1 s from reward, with the time of reward, or 5 s following reward delivery.
source: During peak probe trials, stimulation was delivered at −1 s from reward, with the time of reward, or 5 s following reward delivery.

claim: Licking timestamps were filtered to exclude events occurring less than 8 ms apart.
source: Licking timestamps were filtered to exclude events occurring less than 8 ms apart.

claim: Unless otherwise stated, all analyses were performed on the first half of trials to exclude motivational effects.
source: Unless otherwise stated, all analyses were performed on the first half of trials to exclude motivational effects.

claim: Peak duration had to be at least 2 s in duration and licking rate had to exceed 3 Hz to be included.
source: Peak duration had to be at least 2 s in duration and licking rate had to exceed 3 Hz to be included.
